rationale: A wins because it knows where the evidence stops. Its strongest angle, "Mindbody says texting the waitlist cut studio no-shows 22% in a pilot," is boring in the right way: measurable, beat-shaped, and proof-gated. B has sharper instincts, but "The company that owns ClassPass now decides which classes fill first" turns an unanswered question into a headline, which is how you buy yourself an angry follow-up email from a reporter.
gaps_in_A: "The software behind 50,000 studios" trims the supplied fact; the update says Mindbody powers over 50,000 studios and salons, not 50,000 fitness studios.
"most boutique studios will never buy an AI tool" is plausible context, but it is not in the update and needs sourcing before it becomes the spine of a trend angle.

"The prevailing pattern...is AI as a paid add-on or premium tier" may be true, but the update does not prove it; the angle correctly asks for competitor examples, but the headline still leans on an external claim.
"Next step: journalist-fit-check" is a touch premature. Pilot methodology and a named studio should be pressure-tested before building a media list.
gaps_in_B: "front desks stopped having time to do" invents a staffing/workload story the update does not supply.
"studios get it whether or not they asked for it" confuses bundled pricing with forced rollout or adoption. Those are not the same thing.

"The company that owns ClassPass now decides which classes fill first" is the big overreach. The facts say Mindbody owns ClassPass and has a waitlist/class-time assistant; they do not say the assistant touches ClassPass inventory or member priority.

"a bundled-into-existing-tiers AI feature is a margin and retention play...a recognizable PE playbook" turns take-private status into a private-equity strategy story without evidence. Interesting question, thin angle.
